cues.zh: 它们是极其微小的粒子，是原子的一部分。它们以巨大的力量相互排斥。这股力与距离的平方成反比，就像引力也与距离的平方成反比一样。但引力是吸引的，而这股力是排斥的。对两个电子来说，引力比起电力来实在太微弱了。电力比引力大得多，我都形容不出来，因为我都不知道那个数字叫什么。是1后面跟着38个或40个零，电力比引力大这么多。

cues.en: It's so enormous that if I were all electrons, well, the numbers are too big. So if there's also, however, for electrical things, other kind of charge, positive charges. An example of protons are positive. They're inside the nucleus of the atom, and they attract electrons. Opposite charges attract them. Like charges repel. So you have to imagine enormous forces where likes are trying to get away from likes, and unlikes are trying to get near
cues.zh: 它大到如果我全是由电子构成的——好吧，数字实在太大了。不过电现象中还有另一种电荷，也就是正电荷。比如质子带正电，它们位于原子核内部，吸引着电子。异种电荷相吸，同种电荷相斥。所以你得想象出极其巨大的力，同种电荷竭力避开彼此，异种电荷竭力靠近彼此。

cues.en: The opposite. What would happen if you had a lot of them? They'd be, all the likes would collect with unlikes. They attract each other. And they'd get an intimate mixture of pluses and minuses all on top of each other, very close together. You wouldn't have a lot of pluses anywhere because they repel each other. They'd all be compensated by minuses very close. And you get these little knots of plus and minus. The reason that the knots don't get smaller and smaller is because they are particles and it's got quantum mechanical effects that we wouldn't.
cues.zh: 反过来，如果你有一大堆这样的电荷，会发生什么呢？所有的同种电荷都会和异种电荷聚集在一起，它们相互吸引。于是正负电荷紧密交织、叠在一起，彼此靠得非常近。你不会在任何地方看到大量聚集的正电荷，因为它们互相排斥，它们全都被近在咫尺的负电荷抵消了。于是就形成了这些正负交织的微小团簇。这些团簇没有变得越来越小，是因为它们是粒子，且存在我们不会……的量子力学效应。

cues.en: discussed that makes it that you can't get any smaller than a certain size. And so you get these little lumps, which are balls. They're the atoms. The atoms have positive and negative charge, and they're neutralized. They cancel that charge as nearly as they can. And because of this intimate, this force is so big, it ends up nowhere, with very little left. Because it's so big, it cancels out. There's always exactly the same pluses and minuses in any normal material. When you comb your hair,
cues.zh: 我们讨论过，这使物体不能小于某个尺寸。于是就有了这些小团块，也就是小球。它们就是原子。原子带正负电荷，并且会被中和。它们尽可能抵消掉电荷。由于这种近距离作用，这个力非常大，结果几乎不剩什么。因为它太大，所以会互相抵消。任何普通物质里，正负电荷总是恰好一样多。当你梳头发时，

cues.en: It rubs just a little bit extra or just a few extra minuses say here and somewhere else a few extra pluses But the forces are so big there's just the extra ones which make a force that we can see that seems to be at a long range and that we find mysterious and that we need an explanation for and we try to find an explanation for it in terms of ideas like the forces that are inside of rubber bands or steel bars or twisted things
cues.zh: 它会多擦出一点点，或者说这里多出几个负电荷，别处多出几个正电荷。但这些力太大了，只有那些多出来的电荷才产生我们能看到的力；它看起来像是长程力，我们觉得神秘，需要解释，于是试着用橡皮筋、钢条或扭曲物体内部的力这类概念来解释它。

cues.en: We would like to have some kind of puller at a distance because we're used to it, that we don't get any push until we're touching. But the fact is that the reason we don't get any push until we're touching is it's the same force as you see at a long distance, only it's come down to short because the pluses and minuses have canceled out so well that you don't feel anything until it gets very, very close. When it gets close enough, of course, it makes the difference which is plus and which is minus and where they are and they repel each other. So it's kind of...
cues.zh: 我们想要某种远距离的吸引力，因为我们习惯了它；而直到接触之前，我们感觉不到任何推力。但事实是，直到接触才感到推力的原因在于，这和在远距离看到的力是同一种力，只不过它变成了短程，因为正负电荷抵消得太好，直到靠得非常非常近你才感觉到什么。当它靠得足够近时，当然，哪个是正、哪个是负、它们在哪里就变得重要了，它们会互相排斥。所以这有点……

cues.en: Fun to imagine this intimate mixture of highly attractive opposites, which are so strong that they cancel out the effects. And it's only sometimes when you have an excess of one kind or another that you get this mysterious electrical force. And how can I explain a mysterious electrical force in any other way? Why should I try to explain it in terms of stiff, of something like jelly or...
cues.zh: 想象这种近距离混合的、彼此强烈吸引的对立面，很有意思；它们强到会抵消彼此的效果。只有偶尔某一类电荷多出来时，你才会得到这种神秘的电作用力。我还能用什么别的方式解释神秘的电作用力呢？我为什么要用僵硬的、像果冻一样的东西来解释它，或者……

cues.en: other things which are made and I understand the other way around in terms of strong long-distance forces which have all cancelled out. So it's the electrical forces in fact and the magnetic forces in fact that we have to accept as the base reality in which we're going to explain all the other things. So again it turns out it's hard to understand and you have to do a lot of imagining that the real world has as its base.
cues.zh: 以及其他被造出来的东西；而我是反过来用那些已被完全抵消的强长程力来理解它们的。所以事实上，我们必须把电作用力和磁力当作基础现实来接受，并在此基础上解释其他所有东西。所以又一次，事实证明这很难理解，你必须大量想象现实世界的基础是什么。

cues.en: A force which acts at a long distance that we haven't got much experience with that force. We have peculiar phenomena hanging in there, but ordinarily we don't have much experience with that force. It's simply because that's what requires explanation. That's what requires imagination. The long distance force we have no other picture for. And then the example of the generator, for instance.
cues.zh: 一种作用在远距离上的力，我们对这种力并没有多少经验。我们有一些奇特现象悬在那里，但通常我们对这种力没有多少经验。原因很简单：正是它需要解释。正是它需要想象力。对远距离力，我们没有别的图景。然后比如说发电机的例子。

cues.en: What happens is that the electrons, which are part of an atom, they're pushed by the motion of the copper wires. And it's wonderful to think that you push a few here and they get too close together so they push the others because they repel it a long distance. So it's not just like water which repels it a short distance, but it's a wonderful fluid.
cues.zh: 实际情况是，作为原子一部分的电子，会被铜线的运动所推动。想想看这真的很奇妙：你在这里推几个电子，它们靠得太近，就会因为远距离斥力而推开其他电子。所以它不像水那样只在短距离内排斥，而是一种奇妙的流体。

cues.en: Which we pose at a long distance and the effects therefore can go very quickly through the wire if there's a little concentration you go zing Through the wire all over the city at once and electrical you can use that stuff to make signals You can push all the fuel electrons here and there by talking in a telephone at the other end of the line a long line of copper across the city The electrons respond because of this very rapid interactions over these long distances to what you're saying in this room and it discovered
cues.zh: 这种流体能在远距离产生排斥，因此影响能在导线中极快地传播，只要有一点聚集，“嗖”的一下就瞬间传遍整座城市的导线，你可以利用它来传递电信号。你在电话里讲话，就能在这里或那里推动哪怕一点点电子，穿过横跨整座城市的漫长铜线，电子会因为这种长距离的极速相互作用，对你在房间里说的话做出响应，而发现

cues.en: experimentally, the existence of these long forces and these rapid motion actions and so forth was a tremendous thing for human beings. I think that the discovery of electricity and magnetism and the electromagnetic effects, which finally worked out, the full equations for everything was worked out by Maxwell in 1873, is probably the most fundamental transformation of
cues.zh: 在实验中证实这种长程力的存在，以及这些快速的运动作用等等，对人类来说是一件极其伟大的事情。我认为，电、磁以及电磁效应的发现——最终由 Maxwell 在 1873 年推导出了描述一切的完整方程组——可能算得上是最根本的变革，

cues.en: the most remarkable thing in history, the biggest change in history. I went to a scientific school, MIT, and then fraternity, when you first joined, they tried to keep you from being, if you think you're smart, from feeling that you're too smart by giving you what looked like simple questions to try to figure out what actually happens. And it's like training for imagination. It's kind of fun, and I thought I'd...
cues.zh: 是历史上最非凡的事情，也是历史上最大的变革。我当年上的是理工院校 MIT，刚加入兄弟会的时候，要是你自以为很聪明，他们就会出一些看似简单的问题，让你琢磨到底发生了什么，借此挫挫你的锐气，不让你觉得自己太聪明。这就像是对想象力的训练，挺有意思的，我想……

cues.en: I tell you some of them that I remember. I learned them. Of course, once you learn them, the next time somebody comes along with this wonderful puzzle, you look at them kind of quietly. You wait two or three seconds or five seconds to show whiz that you were thinking. And then you come up with this answer to astonish your friends. But the fact was, of course, that you were trained by your fraternity brothers as to how to answer these things early on. One of the questions we got was the problem about the mirror. It's an old-fashioned. It's an old problem.
cues.zh: 我挑几个记得的给你们讲讲。我弄懂了这些问题。当然，一旦你懂了，下次再有人拿这种妙趣谜题来考你，你就会神色平静地看着他们，等上两三秒甚至五秒，装出一副正在思考的天才模样，然后抛出答案惊艳你的朋友。但事实显然是，兄弟会的前辈们早就训练过你该怎么回答这些问题了。我们当年遇到的一个问题是关于镜子的。这是个老掉牙的、古老的问题。

cues.en: You look in a mirror and let's say you part your hair on the right side and you look in the mirror and the image has got its hair part on the left side. So the image is left to right mixed up. It's not top and bottom mixed up because the top of the head of the image is up there at the top and the bottom of the feet are at the bottom. And the question is how does a mirror know to get the left and right mixed up and not the up and down? You get a better idea of the problem if you think of lying down and looking at the mirror.
cues.zh: 你照镜子，假设你的头发是往右边分缝的，你看镜子里的像，它的头发缝却是在左边。所以镜像是左右颠倒的。但它并不是上下颠倒的，因为镜像里头的头顶依然在最上面，脚底也依然在最下面。问题就来了：镜子怎么就知道该颠倒左右，而不是颠倒上下呢？要是你想象自己躺着照镜子，对这个问题就会有更切身的体会了。

cues.en: All right, your hair is still on the left side. And now the left and right was the up and down. Whereas the up and down, which look OK, was the right and left before. And the mirror somehow figured out what you're going to do when you're looking at it. So to describe in a sort of symmetrical way what a mirror does, that it doesn't look lopsided. And it takes left, it mixes it up with right, and it doesn't do the same with up and down. And after a lot of...
cues.zh: 好，你的头发还在左边。可现在左右变成了上下；而看起来没问题的上下，之前却是左右。镜子不知怎么弄清了你看它时会怎么做。所以要用某种对称的方式描述镜子做了什么，让它看起来不歪斜。它把左和右混在一起，却不对上下做同样的事。后来经过很多……

cues.en: Fiddling, gradually, I knew we worked out the answer to that one. If you wave this hand, then the hand in the mirror that waves is right opposite it. The hand on the east is the hand on the east, and the hand on the west is the hand on the west, and the head that's up is up, and that feet that are down are down. Everything's really all right. But what's wrong is if this is north, your nose is to the north of the back of your head, but in the image, the nose is to the south of the back of the head.
cues.zh: 摆弄来摆弄去，渐渐地，我知道我们弄出了那个问题的答案。你挥这只手，镜子里挥动的手正好在对面。东边的手还是东边的手，西边的手还是西边的手，朝上的头还是朝上，朝下的脚还是朝下。一切其实都没问题。真正不对的是：如果这边是北，你的鼻子在后脑勺的北边，但在镜像里，鼻子在后脑勺的南边。

cues.en: So what happens really in the image is neither the right nor left makes up on the top and bottom But the front and back have been reversed you see that which is the nose on the thing is on the wrong side of the head if you want All right now ordinarily when we think of the image we think of it as another person And we think of the normal way that a person would get into that condition over there. It's a psychological thing We don't think of the idea that the person has been squashed and pushed backwards forwards with his nose and his head because that's not what ordinarily happens to people
cues.zh: 所以在镜像里真正发生的，不是左右变成了上下，而是前后被颠倒了；你看到那个东西的鼻子，可以说长在了脑袋错误的一侧。好，通常我们想到镜像时，会把它当成另一个人，并去想一个人正常会怎样进入那边那个状态。这是心理层面的。我们不会去想这个人被压扁了、连鼻子带脑袋被前后推过去，因为人通常不会变成那样。

cues.en: A person gets to look like he looks in a mirror by walking around and facing you. And because people, when they walk around, don't turn their head for their feet, we leave that part alone. But they get their right and left hands swung about, you see, when they turn around. And so we say that it's left and right interchange. But really, the symmetrical way is along the axis of the mirror that things get interchanged. Well, that's kind of an easy one. A hard one, and very entertaining, was what keeps a train on the track.
cues.zh: 一个人看起来像镜中那样，是因为他转过身来面对你。因为人转身时不会把头相对于脚倒过来，所以那部分我们不管。但他们转身时，左右手会调换位置。于是我们说这是左右互换。但真正对称的方式，是沿着镜子的轴发生互换。嗯，这算简单的。难而又有趣的，是火车为什么能留在轨道上。

cues.en: And, of course, the answer is, as everyone thinks, the flanges on the wheels, you know, the wheels have some kind of flange on them. But that's not the answer. Those flanges are just safety devices. If the flanges rub against the tracks, you hear a terrible squealing. They're just in case the real mechanism doesn't work. There's another problem with trains that's connected to it. People all know this about their automobile, that when you go around the corner, the outside wheels have to go further than the inside wheels.
cues.zh: 当然，答案就像大家以为的那样，是车轮上的轮缘——你知道，车轮上有某种轮缘。但这不是答案。那些轮缘只是安全装置。如果轮缘蹭到轨道，你会听到刺耳的尖叫声。它们只是以防真正机制失效。火车还有另一个相关问题。大家都从汽车上知道：转弯时，外侧车轮必须比内侧车轮走得更远。

cues.en: And if the front, if the wheels were connected on a solid shaft, you couldn't do that. You can't turn the outside wheels further than the inside wheels. And so the shaft is broken in the middle with a gear system, it's called a differential. Did you ever see the differential on a railroad train? No, you look at those wheels under a freight car and there are the two wheels and there's a solid steel rod going from one wheel to the other. There's nothing, one turns the same as the other. So now how does it go around the corner?
cues.zh: 要是轮子是连在一根实心轴上的，你就没法这么干。因为外侧轮子转得肯定比内侧轮子多。所以车轴中间被打断了，加了套齿轮系统，也就是差速器。你在火车上见过差速器吗？没有吧，你去看看货车车厢下面的轮子，就两个轮子，中间连着一根实心钢轴。什么都没有，一个转多少，另一个就转多少。那它到底是怎么拐弯的呢？

cues.en: A curve when the outside wheel has to go further than the inside wheel. And the answer is that the wheels are flanged like this. I mean not flanged, they're cones this way. That is they're a little fatter closer to the train and a little thinner further out. If you look closely you'll see they've got this beveled edge. And it's all very simple when they go around a curve. They slide out on the track a bit so that this wheel travels on a fatter part.
cues.zh: 转弯时外侧轮子走的路程可比内侧多啊。答案是轮子做成了这种带法兰的形状。我是说，不是法兰，其实是锥形的。也就是靠近车身的一侧稍粗一点，靠外的一侧稍细一点。仔细看的话，你会发现它有个斜面。拐弯时的原理其实非常简单。它们会在轨道上稍微往外滑一点，这样外侧轮子就踩在比较粗的部分上，

cues.en: a bigger diameter, and this on a smaller diameter. So when they both turn one turn, this swings further than the other. And that's what keeps it on the track also the same way. Suppose a train's running along on this thing, on the track, and the track's here and here, and the two wheels are exactly balanced, and it's nice and even. Suppose accidentally it gets a bump or something and slides out this way. Then this wheel is on a bigger circumference than this one, but they're on a solid shaft.
cues.zh: 也就是在更大的直径上滚动，而另一个轮子则在较小的直径上。所以当两边各转一圈时，这个走得就比另一个远。这也正是它能保持在轨道上的原因。假设火车在轨道上跑，两边各是一条钢轨，两个轮子刚好平衡，跑得很稳当。假设不小心碰了一下，稍微往这边滑了一点。那这个轮子踩的圆周就比另一个大，可它们连在同一根实心轴上啊。

cues.en: So when it turns once around, it carries this wheel forward, relative to the other, and steers the train back on the track. Of course, if it gets too far off on the other side, it goes back and forth, and it stays on the track because the wheels are tapered, and the flange is safety. Well, we had a lot of stuff like that that we had to learn, you know, to get straightened out before we could become full-fledged members of the fraternity. If I'm sitting next to a swimming pool, somebody dives in, and she's not too pretty.
cues.zh: 所以转上一圈，它就会带动这个轮子相对于另一个向前走，从而把火车重新导向正轨。当然，要是往另一边偏得太厉害，它就会来回晃动，但由于轮子是锥形的，它始终能留在轨道上，法兰只是起个保险作用。总之，我们得弄明白好多诸如此类的事，全搞懂了才能真正算入行。要是我坐在游泳池边，有人跳进水里，而且长得不太好看。

cues.en: So I can think of something else. I think of the waves and things that have formed in the water. And when lots of people have dived in the pool, there's a very great choppiness of all these waves all over the water. And to think that it's possible, maybe, that in those waves is a clue as to what's happening in the pool. That some sort of insect or something with sufficient cleverness could sit in the corner of the pool and just be disturbed by the waves. And by the nature of the irregularities and bumping of the waves have figured out
cues.zh: 那我就能去琢磨点别的事。我想到了水里形成的那些波浪。当很多人跳进泳池时，整个水面上到处都是非常杂乱的波纹。想想看，也许就在这些波浪里，藏着泳池里发生了什么的线索。假如有某种足够聪明的昆虫什么的，坐在泳池角落里，仅仅感受着波浪的起伏。就能从波浪的不规则和震荡特性中推断出

cues.en: who jumped in, where and when, and what's happening all over the pool. And that's what we're doing when we're looking at something. The light that comes out is waves, just like in the swimming pool, except in three dimensions instead of the two dimensions of the pool as they're going in all directions. And we have an eighth of an inch black hole into which these things go, which is particularly sensitive to the parts of the waves that are coming in.
cues.zh: 是谁在何时何地跳了进去，以及整个泳池里正在发生什么。而我们看东西时其实也是在做同样的事。射出来的光就是波，就像游泳池里的水波一样，只不过水波是二维的，而光波是三维的，向四面八方传播。我们眼睛里有一个八分之一英寸的黑洞，这些波会钻进去，它对射进来的这些波格外敏感。

cues.en: a particular direction. It's not particularly sensitive when they're coming in at the wrong angle. What you say is from the corner of our eye. And if we want to get more information from the corner of our eye, we swivel this ball about so that the hole moves from place to place. Then it's quite wonderful that we can figure out so easy. That's really because the light waves are easier than the waves in the water, a little bit more complicated. It would have been harder for the bug than for us. But it's the same idea, to figure out
cues.zh: 某个特定的方向。如果光线射入的角度不对，它就没那么敏感，也就是我们常说的眼角余光。而如果我们想从余光里获取更多信息，就会转动眼球，让瞳孔移到不同的位置。我们能如此轻松地分辨出来，真的很奇妙。这其实是因为光波比水波更容易处理，水波要更复杂一些。小虫子面临的挑战会比我们更难。但原理是相通的，都是要搞清楚
